data.title: Lawmakers urge Army to postpone Iowa lead detonation, citing late communication
data.description:
Federal and state lawmakers are urging the Army to postpone its planned detonation of a lead azide bomb in Iowa, citing late communication on the event. 

“The safety of Iowans now and in the future should be government’s top concern,” Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) wrote on social media. “An unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation.”

“The public deserves to know, if this is the safest option, why other options were worse,” he continued. “If it isn’t as safe as possible to do this tomorrow, it shouldn’t happen tomorrow.”

The Army on Nov. 15 announced in a press release it planned to detonate two degrading lead azide bombs on at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Nov. 20 at around noon. Nearby residents were asked to vacate the area from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. local time.

“While safety measures will be fully enforced, the controlled detonation will cause temporary noise, ground vibrations, and a dust plume that will contain some lead,” the release said. “Residents in Middletown will hear a loud noise; feel vibrations from two consecutive, rapid detonations; and will see a plume of dust.”

Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D-Iowa) said he was “deeply concerned” about the detonations, referencing his father’s past exposure to Agent Orange, an air toxin, which led to him being born with spina bifida.

He expressed that it was also “deeply troubling” that there wasn’t prior notice given from the U.S. Army to outgoing Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) or other public officials.

“As I continue to push for answers and reassurances, I am in communication with Senator Joni Ernst and we are doing all that we can to get clarity,” the incoming senator wrote.

Outgoing Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), who lost against Turek for the Hawkeye State’s open Senate seat, similarly remarked that she believed surrounding communities “were not given adequate notice.”

Turek and Hinson both called for Friday’s detonation to be delayed until the impact on local air quality could be studied. 

The location of the detonation is just over ten miles from the Illinois border, worrying officials in the Prairie State. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D) stated on social platform X that his office was monitoring the planned detonation’s effect on nearby Mercer County and surrounding areas.

data.title: Hawley says he 'has a lot of thinking to do' about possible 2028 presidential bid
data.description:
Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) left the door open to a 2028 presidential bid Thursday despite seemingly ruling one out before the midterms.

Asked by The Associated Press about a possible run for president, Hawley said he has some “thinking to do.”

“After this most recent election, I think everybody that cares about the future of the party, the future of the country, has a lot of thinking to do,” Hawley told the AP. “So I’ll just say I have a lot of thinking to do.”

The comments about a potential 2028 run come despite his previous remarks to the Washington Examiner in September, when he said he had “no intention of doing so, period.”

Jockeying is already underway for the 2028 primaries on both sides, and the GOP is recalibrating after its brutal midterm losses.

Hawley is one of several Republicans who critiqued the president’s job performance and impact on the midterms. Even Vice President Vance, widely considered a top candidate for the GOP nomination, blamed GOP losses on the Iran war.

The Missouri senator occasionally breaks with his party on more populist issues and recently bashed congressional Republicans for how they handled cost of living issues ahead of the midterms.

“What did we do to get the price of gas down? Nothing. What did we do to get the price of healthcare down? Nothing,” Hawley told reporters on Capitol Hill last week. “I think that this party thought we just do whatever we want … No, you can’t.”

Democrats shut down the government last year in protest over proposed GOP cuts to subsidies for the Affordable Care Act, and Hawley was one of four Republicans to vote with Democrats on an extension, but it ultimately failed.

In recent weeks, he said Republicans should use their remaining weeks in the majority to pass a slate of priority bills, but also a moratorium on data centers, something that has support from populists in both parties.

Talking to reporters last week, Hawley said Congress worked for data centers instead of Americans and said lawmakers received a “F” grade from voters.

“I think that this Congress did not come and work for the people,” Hawley said. “This Congress came and worked for AI companies, and it worked for data centers.”

data.title: Fetterman says he's "considering" running for reelection, mocks Lamb and Boyle
data.description:
Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) hinted at running for reelection in 2028 saying he is “considering things.”

“I am considering things,” Fetterman said, when an MS Now reporter Mychael Schnell asked if he is going to run in 2028.

When the reporter asked if he is worried about a primary challenger in 2028, Fetterman responded saying, “Oh … ask [former Rep.] Conor Lamb. What’s he doing?”

Fetterman defeated Lamb in Pennsylvania’s Democratic Senate Primary in 2022.

“You have the little guy from Philly. You can ask him why he chickened out,” he added, referring to Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-Pa.), who said he does not plan to challenge Fetterman in 2028, opting instead to remain in the lower chamber where he’s in line to be the next chairman of the House Budget Committee.

Fetterman recently said signaled during a Fox News interview that he could leave the Democratic party if Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is elected as the Senate Majority Leader, saying, “it would be troubling if my caucus elects someone like Van Hollen that has really made his name being very anti … hostile to Israel.”

Last week, Van Hollen said that he would challenge Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for the role of the majority leader.

“I think he loses … you’ll have to see how that vote goes,” Fetterman told MS Now.

While he considers a reelection bid in 2028, multiple candidates are already lining up to possibly challenge Fetterman for his seat. A poll in August showed Fetterman was more popular among Pennsylvania Republicans than Democrats. 

Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) said Sunday that he is seriously considering a 2028 primary challenge against the current Pennsylvania senator, saying, “Fetterman’s been a mess and he doesn’t take the job seriously. Whatever I decide to do, that guy is not going to be the senator in ’28.”

Ahmed Moor, a Palestinian American writer and businessperson and a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, announced a Senate bid against Fetterman in 2028 Nov. 9, less than a week after the midterm elections where Democrats secured a sweeping victory taking control of both the House and the Senate.

“I’m running to end the war in Iran and to promote the dignity agenda: free healthcare, free childcare, and affordable housing,” Moor wrote on the social platform X.

A day after Moor’s announcement, Rep. Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.) also said she is considering challenging Fetterman, saying, “I have been concerned about, really, two things, which is his family and his health … and am very disappointed in his activity as a senator and in his votes.”

data.title: One company bids to mine off coast of American Samoa after Trump push
data.description:
One company has bid and provisionally won the rights to mine off the coast of American Samoa as the Trump administration pushes for offshore mining.

Wetstone US Ventures provisionally acquired the two leases to mine off the coast, a spokesperson for the Marine Minerals Administration (MMA) said. The company was the only bidder during an auction for the mining rights leases on Thursday.

The area encompasses a combined 31.5 million acres of U.S. federal waters.

Large-scale deep sea mining has never been done before, but it’s something the Trump administration has pushed for as another avenue for shoring up U.S. supply chains. 

“American manufacturers rely on critical minerals to build advanced electronics, energy infrastructure and equipment for our national defense, but heavy reliance on overseas suppliers leaves manufacturers vulnerable when those supplies are disrupted. That’s why this sale is a critical first step in our offshore energy strategy,” said acting MMA director Mike Olsen ahead of the auction.  

Environmental organizations have opposed such efforts, warning that they could be harmful to ocean ecosystems. 

“This premature push to exploit the deep sea before we even fully understand how vital it is will have catastrophic consequences that reverberate for generations,” said Oceana Defense Campaign Manager Julia Singer in a written statement. “The Trump administration has clearly put corporate interests above the health and well-being of our oceans.”

Meanwhile, the leases also face a potential legal snafu. A federal judge ruled this week that the administration did not adequately consider the potential impacts to endangered species.

While her ruling did not explicitly block the lease sale from happening, judge Jill Otake also said in a separate but related case that “any bidders for the leases will be on notice” that the administration violated the Endangered Species Act.

An MMA spokesperson said via email that in order to address the issues raised by the court, the agency has “initiated formal incremental step consultation” with the National Marine Fisheries Service that covers more than the initial Endangered Species Act review.

data.title: Judge rules Trump's defamation case against New York Times, Penguin Random House may proceed
data.description:
President Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The New York Times and publisher Penguin Random House can proceed, a federal judge ruled Thursday — a win in the president’s push to paint the news outlet’s reporting about him as misinformation.

Trump sued over a 2024 book written by two Times reporters, Russ Buettner and Susanne Craig, and published by Penguin Random House. The investigative narrative, titled “Lucky Loser,” recounts the president’s ascent to prominence in the real estate sector.

In the ruling, U.S. District Court Judge Steven D. Merryday, a former President George H. W. Bush appointee, examined the Supreme Court’s landmark New York Times v. Sullivan ruling — which set the standard for defamation lawsuits. He said that, under this precedent, the president may be able to prove the reporters made knowingly false statements about him.

“Anyone who publishes the claim that someone else has committed a crime of the complex nature described in some of the challenged statements … necessarily proceeds with particularized reason to doubt the truth of their statements and with knowledge of a high degree of probable falsity of the statements,” Merryday wrote. 

“In other words, they know that they don’t know, but they are undeterred,” he added.

The Times had sought to dismiss Trump’s claims over the “actual malice” standard for public figures making defamation claims. While ordinary plaintiffs only need to prove a statement’s falsity, lawsuits coming from public figures must also show the respondent acted with the knowledge that what they said was untrue — or acted with a “reckless disregard” for the truth.

In a statement to The Hill, Times spokesperson Charlie Stadtlander vowed to continue to fight Trump’s lawsuit while also praising the judge for dismissing some of his claims

“We continue to believe the remaining claim in the filing has no legal merit. We look forward to making this argument as we continue to defend ourselves against this baseless attack on The Times and the rights of the free and independent press in this country,” Stadtlander said.

Trump has frequently railed against the media throughout his time in and out of office, even briefly barring journalists from accessing White House grounds over their coverage. The president has also sued numerous media organizations for their reporting with mixed success.

His past lawsuits against the Times and the Wall Street Journal were dismissed, the former happening in Merryday’s court. Still, he was able to extract settlements out of CBS News and ABC News after his 2024 win and is engaged in another challenge against the BBC, which he similarly accused of libel.

data.title: Becerra suggests prosecutions for AI attacks
data.description:
California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra (D) on Thursday suggested that humans behind AI cyberattacks should face prosecution.

“If some of these incursions that we’ve seen by these AI agents have been done by human beings, we’d have filed criminal charges against those individuals,” Becerra said in an interview at Politico Pub at the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum.

“Because it’s a machine doesn’t mean you shouldn’t also have the ability to prosecute when malfeasance, when bad things are done,” the Golden State’s former attorney general under former Gov. Jerry Brown (D) and outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) added.

Becerra said he hopes state legislators concur with Newsom’s proposal on Wednesday to give California officials the authority to shut down dangerous AI models, something the incoming governor said he hopes to move swiftly in Sacramento after taking office in January.

“This report by the governor and his team gives us a nice blueprint to work off of, and then we build it from there,” he told Politico.

The remarks come days after Becerra’s successor as attorney general, Rob Bonta (D), sued OpenAI for allegedly placing public safety at risk with its advanced AI models, claiming it had no guardrails to prevent the breach of technology startup Hugging Face.

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told The Hill that the lawsuit singled out OpenAI over an issue that “every major AI lab” has identified.

Becerra, who defeated Republican former Fox News host Steve Hilton earlier this month in the race to lead the Golden State, campaigned with a long list of proposals on how California will approach AI going forward.

His campaign website states that under his leadership, there will be expanded efforts to ensure Californians are literate about the advanced technology, have the state invest in helping workers find jobs who are at risk of losing them to AI and that data centers are more environmentally friendly with an “economic-forward standard.”

“California has the nation’s strongest AI safety laws,” Becerra said on his campaign website. “I will ensure existing requirements are actively enforced, close the gaps that allow bad actors to evade accountability, and work closely with technologists, workers, industry and communities to review, track and strengthen standards as the technology evolves. Good rules mean nothing without monitoring and enforcement.”

Fears about AI’s capabilities have grown, even after many speculated that a recent spate of outages affecting various companies over the last week were due to cyberattacks. U.S. intelligence leaders have dismissed these claims, with some outages likely being due to patches in the company’s software.

Google warned that the world has entered a stage where autonomous AI models, not necessarily prompted by humans, pose a risk. The company’s Google Threat Intelligence Group flagged several trends based on incidents involving AI models in recent months, including cyber espionage and impacts on supply chain systems.

data.title: Exiting GOP senators become liability for Trump
data.description:
Senate Republicans are set to lose eight members in January, and a few of them are not going easy.  

These members have become occasional critics of the administration, more willing to hold up President Trump’s agenda or personnel when they see a need for it.  

The pattern reflects the major loss Trump took in the midterm elections, as blind loyalty to the president was generally a vulnerability for Republicans.

Now, some of the Republicans who lost their seats are more open to exercising their power to rebuke Trump choices they see as unwise. 

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), who lost his primary in May to Trump-backed Rep. Julia Letlow (R-La.), was among the Republicans on the Senate health committee who on Wednesday rejected Jim O’Neill, a science and technology investor and Trump’s nominee to lead the National Science Foundation.  

Cassidy, who has become a fierce critic of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., said the vote to advance O’Neill had been cancelled due a lack of support.   

O’Neill “did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements” from Kennedy, Cassidy said. He noted he was not the only committee member who harbored such concerns. 

“I like Jim personally, but this time requires leadership and fortitude and standing up for what is right,” Cassidy said.  

Prior to O’Neill, Cassidy had voted to advance every Trump health nominee who appeared in front of his committee, overcoming any misgivings. 

Cassidy also had concerns about Heidi Overton, Trump’s nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration, but seemed ready to vote for her anyway until the White House suddenly withdrew her nomination the night before her scheduled hearing. 

Cassidy’s relationship with President Trump has been complicated. The Louisiana senator voted to convict the president in 2021 following the Jan. 6 Capitol attack, but has tried to show he is still loyal, including by casting the deciding vote to confirm Kennedy as HHS Secretary.

But since he lost his reelection bid, Cassidy has repeatedly clashed with Kennedy. 

In an interview on “Face the Nation” on Sunday, Cassidy called Kennedy’s tenure at HHS “a series of failures,” although he stopped short of saying he regretted his vote for the secretary. 

Cassidy, as a committee chair, is uniquely positioned to intervene on controversial nominees. 

But the structure and traditions of the Senate allow individual senators who want to make a statement to exert significant influence. That could foreshadow more pushback from outgoing Republicans, who have little left to lose, on Trump policies and people.  

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) recently used his power as a home-state senator to disapprove of T. Elliot Gaiser, a Trump nominee to be a district judge in Texas.  

Cornyn said he opposed Gaiser because he is not from Texas and does not have trial experience. 

Cornyn’s office said he had recommended another nominee to the administration months ago.  

He then did not submit a “blue slip,” which is essentially a stamp of approval from a senator for judicial nominees in their state. 

“I just refuse to be jammed by a non-Texan who has no trial experience, who hasn’t been vetted,” Cornyn told CNN this week. “And so, we provided the White House an alternative, and I’m hoping they take advantage of it because I don’t want the seat to go vacant either.”  

Gaiser’s nomination will likely not go forward without Cornyn’s approval.  

The move has garnered the outgoing senator plenty of criticism from others on the right, including Heritage Foundation President Kevin Roberts, who lambasted Cornyn online for the move. 

“John Cornyn is going out as the Republican Texas Senator who helped get radical leftist James Talarico’s agenda started early. What a legacy,” Roberts wrote on social media on Thursday, responding to a news article about the Gaiser nomination.  

He earned a sharp reply back from Cornyn: “Kevin, your sycophancy has destroyed the credibility of a once great institution, and in so doing you have made yourself irrelevant.” 

A third Trump pick is also likely to not advance further, after retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) placed a hold on Michael LoSapio, nominated to be the new director for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.  

Tillis objected to LoSapio after the nominee said in his confirmation hearing that the Capitol was not attacked on Jan. 6, 2021.

data.title: Justice Department urges federal judge to let two-year Kennedy Center closure go forward
data.description:
The Justice Department (DOJ) on Thursday defended a decision by the Kennedy Center board to shutter the performing arts center for a planned two-year renovation, telling a federal judge in Washington, D.C., that a non-phased approach was chosen to minimize costs and disruptions to operations.

“The board’s decisions here were reasonable, and they must stand,” Will Jankowski, an attorney in DOJ’s Civil Division, said minutes into the hearing. 

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper is weighing a request by the Trump administration to dissolve a preliminary injunction from May that blocked the proposed closure while allowing “necessary maintenance and repair work” to continue.  

The judge did not, however, permanently bar the board from ever closing the Kennedy Center “should it come to this decision anew after independently balancing its multiple obligations to the Center in a prudent fashion.” 

“It did those things,” Jankowski said, claiming that the board relied on independent assessments from construction firms and real estate experts to make its determination.  

Trump’s handpicked board voted again in September to immediately close the main building for repairs after officials said dilapidated conditions have made it unsafe for visitors. 

Public access to the venue was temporarily cut off a day later, a decision Executive Director Matt Floca said in court filings was made after determining there were “acute risks to public safety” due to structural damage in certain parts of the performing arts center.  

DOJ lawyers have defended that move as independent of the board’s decision to pursue longer-term renovations.  

Lawyers for Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex-officio board member who’s been leading the charge against Kennedy Center changes, argue that the closure was a cover for financial mismanagement and “foreordained” to please Trump.  

“We know that one of the reasons they want to close is because they face fiscal harms and embarrassment as a result of the renaming,” Nathaniel Zelinksy said on Thursday.  

Several artistic partners ended their affiliations with the Kennedy Center and a slew of performers cancelled or withdrew from shows after the board voted last December to inscribe Trump’s name on the facility. The Washington Post also reported in August that ticket sales and fundraising had plummeted in the months since.  

Beatty’s team has also pushed for access to records about Trump’s involvement in the decision-making process as chairman of the board, a demand the White House has rebuffed by asserting executive privilege over some of president’s communications with advisers and Kennedy Center staff.  

Cooper has ordered the Justice Department to turn copies of those documents over to the court by Friday so that he can review them in private and assess the administration’s claim.  

He appeared skeptical of both sides’ arguments, at one point asking Zelinsky “what good” it would be to keep the venue open if no performances are scheduled.  

“Wouldn’t that cause even more financial deterioration at this point, regardless of who’s to blame for it?” Cooper asked.  

The administration, including Trump, has refused to rule out the possibility of razing the building if the president’s name cannot be added and plans for a longer closure are blocked. He was spotted through the window of Air Force One in mid-September looking at a poster board that appeared to say “Kennedy Center DEMOLISH” on it. 

“I’m not committing to anything. We’re going to see how it plays out in court,” Trump said in Sept. 28 interview with TIME magazine. “But if I build it, and if I agree that for the rest of my life, I’m going to be putting up $100 million to have it open to people … then I think the Trump administration should be recognized.” 

The DOJ has suggested in court filings that Trump’s name is inextricably tied to fundraising efforts, while critics argue the president and his allies are attempting to hold the institution hostage. 

“The president is putting a gun to the head of the center,” Zelinsky said. 

Jankowski argued name recognition for fundraising efforts was “the kind of thing that nonprofits do all the time,” to which the judge responded that was a “different scenario” than alleged in this case. 

“Isn’t that more of a form of, you know, taking actions that are contrary to the trust?” Cooper pressed, referencing the assertion that donations could be clawed back if a certain outcome doesn’t happen. “How does that jive with one’s fidelity to the trust?” 

The current closure has forced the upcoming Kennedy Center Honors to be moved to an off-site location in the nation’s capital for the first time in its history.  

Next month’s ceremony honoring Playwright David Mamet, songwriter Paul Anka, composer David Foster, actor Andy Garcia and country music singer Barbara Mandrell is instead being held at Capital One Arena. 

Cooper did not issue a ruling from the bench, indicating that he would rule “as soon as I can.”

data.title: Fed's Jefferson says AI buildout 'exerting upward pressure' on inflation
data.description:
Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said Thursday the artificial intelligence buildout is putting “upward pressure” on prices, while adding the technology could lower prices in the future by boosting productivity.

During an International Monetary Fund and Central Bank of Brazil conference, Jefferson said AI is “likely to automate some tasks and augment others” in the long-term. 

“Currently, the AI buildout is exerting upward pressure on demand and inflation,” the Fed vice chair said.

“In the future, advancements in productivity could exert downward pressure on inflation while continuing to support growth,” he added.

Jefferson also noted energy price shocks from the nearly nine-month Iran war are contributing to inflation. While gas prices are down relative to a month ago, the average price of a gallon of regular gas is roughly 63 cents higher than it was a year, AAA reported Thursday.

Energy prices increased by 0.7 percent from September to October, after rising by 5.2 percent percent from August to September, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

The increase in energy prices in the early months of the war contributed to overall inflation rising, as annual inflation remains above the Fed’s 2 percent target rate.

To combat persistent inflation, officials on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raised interest rates by a quarter point in September. In late October, the FOMC held rates steady at a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent.

While Jefferson did not forecast his vote at the FOMC’s next meeting, set for Dec. 8-9, he warned about inflation risks “becoming unanchored.”

If that occurs, he argued a “stronger reaction” from the central bank is “warranted.”

Traders are pricing in a 96.4 percent chance of FOMC officials raising rates by a quarter point next month, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

data.title: Trump administration approved shipment of 900,000 AI chips to China
data.description:
The Trump administration approved the shipment of nearly 900,000 AI chips to Defense Department-designated Chinese military companies, according to newly released documents from the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

The documents revealed the U.S. signed off on the sale of 879,868 AI semiconductor chips from Nvidia and AMD. The specific chips sold were Nvidia’s sensitive H200 chips along with their AMD equivalent. 

The order was fulfilled through 21 license applications as of May 11 – including sending 75,000 to Alibaba, 150,000 to Tencent and its subsidiaries, 43,000 to Baidu and 4,000 to BYD. The four companies were all identified on the Defense Department’s 2026 list of alleged Chinese military companies operating in the U.S.

The committee wrote that under the Export Control Reform Act, Rep. Brian Mast (R-Fla.), chair of the panel, was able to “publicly reveal export control license application information” related to Nvidia and AMD’s AI chip licenses for China. 

Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), ranking member on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, accused the Trump administration of mishandling chip export controls, saying it “has put our national security and technology edge at risk.”

He also bashed the Bureau of Industry and Security for failing “to enforce the rules,” adding that “Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration’s policies.”

An Nvidia spokesperson told The Hill, “the review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes.”

“Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China,” the spokesperson added. 

AMD did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment. 

Mast has led probes in the House into the Trump administration’s approval of Nvidia’s H200 chips last year. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang previously argued to federal government officials that the sale of its third or fourth best chips would make China dependent on the U.S.-made infrastructure.
